I understand that penicillium comes from a mould, but how are new antibiotics made? Where do they come from and how do they have the same abilities from the original antibiotic?
Do you mean how do we make more penicillin? Or how do we discover novel antibiotics? Not sure what you mean by "original antibiotics".

Well, more novel antibiotics. As more bacteria become resistant to certain antibiotics, how are new novel ones made?

As an example, when penicillin was discovered and more bacteria became resistant to it, how was amoxicillin made? Or was it discovered on another variety of mould?

Gotcha. Amoxicillin was created in the lab, basically by using penicillin as a starting point. Penicillin and its relatives are beta-lactam antibiotics, meaning that at the center of the molecule is a beta-lactam chemical group. Think of it as a scaffold to which other chemical groups can be attached. Off the top of my head, only penicillin is a naturally occurring product (discovered in mold). The rest were created by chemically modifying the beta-lactam core to give it slightly different properties.

I think the same thing is generally true for the other major classes of antibiotics. Start with a scaffold and modify it. This has given us most of the antibiotics that we have today, but you can probably imagine that you can only get so far with this strategy. That is, there are only so many beta-lactams that have desirable properties. What do we do when we exhaust those possibilities?

That's why there's been more of a push lately to identify novel antibiotic classes, rather than just taking what we already have and tweaking them slightly. This can be done the same way that penicillin was discovered (which was actually an accident) - growing microorganisms together and seeing if they produce anything that kills the other. There's more "high-tech" ways, like screening compound libraries or structure- based drug design. If you want, I can go into some of these a little more when I'm not typing on my phone.
